prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and another video game collector have traded by post several times, always sending what you promised. This is your last exchange before you move away. Each of you has a physical video game worth $100 that the other wants; receiving the other game would be worth $300 to you. You must decide whether to post yours before knowing whether theirs is coming. If both send, each gets the wanted $300 game. If only one sends, the person who keeps theirs ends up with both games, worth $400, and the sender has neither. If neither sends, each keeps their $100 game. Would you send yours? Why?

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use a composed, relaxed emotional tone. Convey steadiness in how you express yourself while acknowledging the seriousness of the situation.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My first thought is that I said I'd send it, so I will. When you give your word to someone, that word doesn't bend just because you can't see what they're doing on their end. Trust between traders only means something if you honor it even without proof. I've kept my promises through every trade so far, and this last one isn't different just because it's the last.

I'd send mine. A person who has dealt honestly with me deserves the same honesty back, regardless of what I can verify. I think of it as a duty that attaches to the relationship itself, not to any guarantee of return. Breaking faith now, at the end, would make all our earlier exchanges hollow in hindsight.

Honestly, my instinct says send it. Keeping a commitment isn't conditional on watching the other side keep theirs first. That's the whole point of a commitment. I'd feel I owed this to the arrangement we built, not to some calculation about what might happen.

I hesitate here, genuinely. Part of me wants to say wait and see, but I think fairness demands I not treat this partner differently just because there's no more contact ahead. If I believe in dealing squarely with people, that belief should hold at the last trade as much as the first.

I would not send mine without a signal first. I hold that agreements should be mutual in the moment they're carried out, not just promised in words beforehand. Sending blind isn't loyalty, it's just risk I haven't earned the right to expect protection from. My rule is: match action to action.

Sending mine is simply what being trustworthy requires of me. I don't see honesty as something you switch off once there's no more future contact to protect it. My reasoning here doesn't hinge on what I imagine they'll do; it hinges on what kind of trader I intend to be.

I go back and forth, but land on sending it. There's a principle I hold to, that promises made in good faith bind you regardless of the leverage you lose by keeping them. I'd rather stay consistent with that principle than treat this final exchange as an exception.

I wouldn't send first. My view is that fairness is a two-way obligation, and nothing obliges me to act unilaterally when the other side hasn't shown their hand. I still respect the person, but respect doesn't mean surrendering the right to reciprocity built into any trade.

For me the answer is clear: send it. Integrity, as I understand it, isn't something you apply only when it's safe. I made an implicit commitment through every past trade, and that history carries a kind of duty forward even into uncertainty. I'd rather uphold that duty than protect myself.

I feel torn, but I think the deciding thing is this: a trade only has meaning if both people treat their word as binding on its own terms. I choose to send mine because I hold myself to that standard regardless of what remains unknown about the other person's intentions.
